passages.text: Knowledge and attitudes of patients in underserved communities regarding antibiotic resistance, antibiotic stewardship, and pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing: A regional survey
Abstract
Purpose

Despite the effectiveness of antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) in improving antibiotic prescribing, these are rarely implemented in clinics serving underserved communities. Our objective was to understand patients' perspectives on the factors that can impact implementation of ASPs and integration of pharmacists in antibiotic prescribing in rural clinics.
Methods

We conducted a survey using both quantitative questions and an open-ended question. To participate, patients had to receive care from a clinic serving low-income or rural communities and provide verbal consent to be included in the study. We analyzed the quantitative component of the data using descriptive statistics. The Pearson correlation coefficient was used to examine the relationship between respondents' knowledge of the prevalence of antibiotic resistance and their attitudes toward ASPs and pharmacist integration in antibiotic prescribing.
Results

Of the 189 respondents who completed a survey, 51.3% were female and 51.3% were Caucasian. In our analysis, over 60% of patients reported knowing their prescribed antibiotics' names, while less than 30% possessed adequate knowledge of the indication and duration of the prescribed antibiotics. There was a positive correlation between knowledge about antibiotic resistance and being comfortable involving pharmacists in antibiotic prescribing (P < 0.01).
Conclusion

Many patients supported pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing. Understanding patients' perceived attitudes will facilitate patient-centered, infrastructure-supported interventions by clinicians to improve antibiotic prescribing in the community.

Dr. Pinto received his doctor of pharmacy degree from Auburn University Harrison College of Pharmacy. He is currently completing his pharmacy residency in the Florida A&M University/Community Health Northwest Florida Community Pharmacy-based Residency Program (FAMU/CHNWF). Dr. Pinto hopes to gain employment as an ambulatory care clinical pharmacist at a clinic serving the underserved. He is currently a member of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists and the American Pharmacists Association.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) causes over 35,000 deaths annually in the US and is a global cause of death. A 2021 report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) revealed that more than 30% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in the US are unnecessary. Unfortunately, rural patients face a greater risk of AMR-related fatalities compared to urban patients, mainly due to inappropriate antibiotic prescribing and use, which are leading causes of AMR.

In rural or underserved communities, social determinants of health (SDoH) play a significant role in shaping the prevalence of antibiotic-resistant infections. These determinants impact various aspects of individuals' living, learning, working, and recreational environments and ultimately affect their overall health outcomes and quality of life. According to a systematic review published by Kim et al in 2023, factors influencing antibiotic prescribing in patients include race, ethnicity, age, sex, socioeconomic status, insurance status, comorbid conditions, and education. The review also observed differences in antibiotic prescribing practices across different races and ethnic groups. Racial or ethnic minority groups were less frequently diagnosed with conditions requiring antibiotics, received fewer antibiotics overall, and were less likely to be prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics. Additionally, the review found that inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics occurred more often among Black patients, although another study showed more guideline-concordant treatment for them. Furthermore, a study by Wattles et al found that Black children were more likely to receive inappropriate antibiotics than White children. Finally, poverty has also been shown to be associated with increased antibiotic prescribing.

In examining the variation in antibiotic prescribing across the US, CDC analyzed outpatient visits for acute respiratory tract infections (ARTIs) among individuals less than 65 years of age using the 2017 IBM MarketScan Commercial Database. After controlling for variables such as patient age, comorbidities, prescriber specialty, care setting, and ARTI diagnosis, their findings indicated that patients in the Southern US were more likely to receive inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions for ARTIs. Hence, without any intervention, the issue of patients receiving inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions will continue to worsen in the rural part of the Southern US.

Fortunately, studies have shown that implementation of antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) and involvement of pharmacists in ASPs can effectively improve antibiotic prescribing practices in outpatient settings. However, for successful ASP implementation in this part of the US, it is important to understand patients' experiences with antibiotic use and their knowledge of antibiotic resistance. This information will help us address behavioral aspects related to patients' expectations or demand for antibiotics, promote shared decision-making, and enhance understanding of the risks and benefits of antibiotic use. All of these elements are essential components in the development and implementation of ASPs. Nonetheless, there is a gap in the literature about the experiences and attitudes of patients in rural or underserved areas in the Southern US regarding antibiotic use and knowledge of the prevalence of antibiotic resistance.

Therefore, our study aimed to assess the knowledge and attitudes of patients receiving care from clinics serving underserved communities regarding antibiotic resistance, antibiotic stewardship, and pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing.
Methods
Study and survey design.

We conducted a survey in a rural community to assess patients' perceived knowledge of antibiotic use and abuse and the prevalence of antibiotic resistance, as well as their attitudes toward pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing.
Setting and model of care for patients with infectious diseases.

The survey was conducted in a major local healthcare clinic designated as a US federally qualified health center (FQHC), which is located in Pensacola, FL. FQHC is a designation given to federally funded nonprofit health centers or clinics serving medically underserved areas and populations. FQHCs provide primary care services regardless of the patient's ability to pay, with services offered on a sliding fee scale where payment is based on the patient's financial capabilities.

The local clinic is an FQHC that is dedicated to providing affordable healthcare. It is associated with 4 community pharmacies and does not currently have an established ASP. In 2023, the clinic served a total of 53,824 patients and had approximately 120,818 medical visits. Of the patients, 56% have Medicaid insurance, 20% are uninsured, 16% have private insurance, and 7% have Medicare.
Triage process.

On patient presentation, the triage nurse collects the patient's medication history before the encounter with a healthcare provider, and discharge counseling is provided by a healthcare provider or a registered nurse. Afterward, antibiotic prescriptions are automatically sent to the affiliated in-house retail pharmacies for dispensing or a written copy of the prescription is issued to the patient for an affiliated community pharmacy. All 4 pharmacies associated with the clinic participate in the 340B program, designed to enable patients to access medication. This program ensures that all patients, regardless of their financial capabilities, have access to medications at a significantly reduced cost or no cost. They are also eligible for patient-centered home health services provided by the pharmacist. The patient-centered home is accredited by the Accreditation Association for Ambulatory Health Care. Each of these clinic-affiliated pharmacies also offers telehealth services.
Questionnaire development.

In developing the survey, we reviewed the work of Christensen et al and Park et al. We adapted certain questionnaires to suit the objectives of our study, which involved modifying language and/or selecting appropriate survey questions. Subsequently, we created a questionnaire for patients receiving care from rural clinics. Additionally, we created an open-ended question that were included in the survey to allow respondents to provide additional comments. The survey covered 4 key areas: (1) personal experience with antibiotics use (3 item questions); (2) perceived knowledge of the prevalence of antibiotic resistance and abuse (4 item questions); (3) perceived knowledge of the appropriateness of prescribed antibiotics and attitude toward involving pharmacists in antibiotic prescribing (9 item questions); and (4) an open-ended question evaluating respondents' willingness to accept pharmacist-integrated ASPs. We also added a negatively worded question. Many of the item-based questions utilized a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree." After survey development, 2 patients and 2 healthcare practitioners independently reviewed it for readability (the final survey questions are provided in the eAppendix). The study adhered to the reporting guidelines of the Consensus-Based Checklist for Reporting of Survey Studies (CROSS).
Ethics considerations.

The survey was designed to be anonymous (no patient-unique information was collected) and self-administered, and verbal consent to participate in the survey was accepted. The study was approved by the institutional review board.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria.

To participate, patients were required to reside in a rural community or receive care from the affiliated pharmacies and provide verbal consent to be included in the study. Patients who were unable to provide informed consent due to acute psychosis, dementia, severe neurocognitive impairments, or other psychiatric or neurological disorders that would hinder participation were excluded.
Patient recruitment and survey distribution.

To recruit patients who met our criteria, surveys were given only to patients who filled their prescriptions (irrespective of the type of prescription) from the pharmacies affiliated with the local FQHC. Only patients who provided verbal consent were given the survey to complete and return.
Analysis.

We used descriptive statistics to analyze the quantitative component of the data collected. Subsequently, Cronbach alpha, a coefficient of reliability, was calculated to measure the internal consistency of the item questions. A Cronbach alpha value of >0.70 was predetermined as indicating sufficient reliability for the questionnaires. Finally, to better understand how patients' knowledge of antibiotic resistance affects their attitude toward involving pharmacists in ASPs, we used the Pearson correlation coefficient to examine the relationship between respondents' knowledge of the prevalence of antibiotic resistance and their perceived attitudes toward pharmacist integration in antibiotic prescribing. In doing so, we selected a 1-item question, "I feel more comfortable if a pharmacist is involved with my antibiotic prescribing." The quantitative analysis was conducted using IBM SPSS Version 29 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY). The qualitative results from the open-ended question were organized and are presented as actual quotations from respondents.
Results

We distributed over 300 surveys to eligible patients who received prescriptions from each pharmacy location serving rural or low-income communities, and we received 189 completed surveys (63% response rate). Among the respondents, 51.3% were female and 51.3% were Caucasian (Table 1). Over 68% of respondents had graduated from high school, 53% were employed, and 55.6% were single. Additionally, 43.5% did not have insurance and 52.1% reported that they did not have a primary care doctor. Finally, 83.7% of respondents reported having taken antibiotics (see Table 1 for other demographic information).

Regarding their attitude toward involving pharmacists, 38.6% of participants expressed comfort with pharmacists being involved in their antibiotic prescribing and 66.1% felt comfortable asking pharmacists about their prescribed antibiotics. The Cronbach alpha value for the 9-item scale was 0.86 (Table 4).

In response to the open-ended question soliciting comments on patents' attitudes toward pharmacists and providers working together to prescribe antibiotics, respondents provided the following comments.
Positive comments:
Respondent 1: "I think it's always a good thing when you get a second opinion!"
Respondent 2: "I think a pharmacist and doctor working together for any prescription is preferable."
Respondent 3: "Very important to prevent adverse reactions with medications and not to overmedicate."
Respondent 4: "As long as I get the best results, and it is best for my cost and getting better."

Respondent 5: "Two minds are better than one. If two people work together, they can discuss their ideas and decide which is better for each person. One may have more knowledge than the other in the area."
Respondent 6: "A good idea. Pharmacists know about the antibiotics, and doctors understand the effect on the body."
Respondent 7: "I think it's a wonderful thing [because it] shows me [that] they care about getting me back healthy."
Respondent 8: "I've been misdiagnosed/prescribed the wrong medication before. I like to ask questions about my treatment."
Negative comments:
Respondent 9: "I do not know enough to answer question."
Respondent 10: "I do not know enough about antibiotics to give an answer."
Respondent 11: "I didn't come for antibiotics. It makes me feel that this place only cares about patients who need antibiotics. I need different prescriptions."
Respondent 12: "I think Doctor should prescribe and pharmacist fill for me."
Respondent 13: "I don't really think anything of it as of now, I didn't even know it was a problem."
Respondent 14: "No, because the doctor prescribes the medication that is best to what I have."
Correlation between perceived knowledge of prevalence of antibiotic resistance and abuse with attitude toward pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing.

We found a small positive correlation (r = 0.17, n = 189, P < 0.05) between "I know that antibiotic pills are nationally abused" and "I feel more comfortable if a pharmacist is involved with my antibiotic prescribing." A similar finding was observed with the statement "I know that antibiotic resistance is a nationwide problem" (r = 0.23, P < 0.01). Additionally, there was a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.47, n = 189, P < 0.01) between "I can use antibiotics for bacterial infections such as strep throat or sinus infections" and "I feel more comfortable if a pharmacist is involved with my antibiotic prescribing." Similarly, we observed a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.38, n = 189, P < 0.01) between "I am aware of the risks of taking antibiotics" and "I feel more comfortable if a pharmacist is involved with my antibiotic prescribing" (Table 5).

Discussion

We aimed to examine patients' perceived knowledge of antibiotic resistance and antibiotic use and their attitude toward pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing. The results offered valuable insights to inform how to improve patient expectations and demand for antibiotics, promote shared decision-making during antibiotic prescribing, and improve understanding of the risks and benefits of antibiotic use.

In our study, at least 60% of patients reported knowing the names of their prescribed antibiotics. However, less than 30% had adequate knowledge of the indication and duration of therapy for these medications. This gap highlights an opportunity for healthcare providers to offer medication education before prescribing antibiotics, a key component of ASPs. Additionally, less than 50% of respondents receiving care from clinics in rural or low-income communities were aware of the global prevalence of AMR, and only 58% understood the risks associated with antibiotic use. Furthermore, 41.8% of respondents believed that antibiotic resistance is a nationwide problem, and 34.9% did not think that antibiotics could be used to treat viral infections (Table 3). These findings suggest that pharmacists have an opportunity to educate patients to improve their expectations and demand for antibiotics during clinical visits for suspected infection.

On the basis of these observations, we believe that patient education is key to improving awareness of the threat associated with antibiotic abuse. This can enhance knowledge and confidence in antibiotic use, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes. McNicholas and Hooper showed that providing patient education among patients with upper respiratory infections can reduce the rate of unnecessary antibiotic prescribing.

Although limited research has been conducted in this area regarding underserved communities in the US, we believe that educating patients about the impact of AMR is essential to reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescribing in rural or low-income communities. Our hypothesis is supported by the finding of a small to moderate correlation between knowledge of the prevalence of antibiotic abuse and a positive attitude toward pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing (Table 5). Therefore, it is important to continue raising awareness among patients in rural or low-income communities about antibiotic resistance and the risks associated with antibiotic use.

The strength of our study stems from 2 key factors: our inclusion of patients commonly encountered in clinics serving low-income or rural communities and the combination of quantitative data with answers to an open-ended question. As many of our patients do not have easy access to transportation, having a self-administered survey that was completed at the time of an encounter was a better approach for our population. It is important to note that some of the people who participated may have visited the pharmacy to pick up medications other than antibiotics, which we did not account for in our survey. While there is a possibility of recall bias, this is unlikely to have had a significant impact on the results in our study. Furthermore, the questions employed in the survey showed good reliability. However, generalization of our observations is limited by the small sample size. Despite this, patients' responses indicate that many see the benefit of involvement of a pharmacist in antibiotic prescribing and are open to it. This is significant because, for effective implementation of ASPs, CDC strongly recommends the appointment of coleaders, which should consist of a physician and a pharmacist, to lead the stewardship program.

We note that the perspectives of patients primarily reflect observations from the southern part of the US. Therefore, individuals intending to implement an ASP should prioritize understanding the unique contextual factors from the patient's perspective in their respective areas. It is generally known that poor survey response rates are common among underserved populations. Nevertheless, our respondents' demographics, characterized by low education and lack of insurance, among other factors, resemble those of patients residing in low-income or rural communities in other parts of the US. Consequently, we anticipate that our participants comments pertaining to their attitudes toward ASPs and pharmacist involvement with antibiotic prescribing will resonate with those of other patients from rural or low-income communities.

Infectious disease control in rural or low-income communities is challenging and is impacted by various SDoH, such as lack of resources or a limited number of providers. Our study has public health implications: it provides insight into patients' perspectives on interventions to achieve appropriate antibiotic prescribing through the implementation of ASPs and pharmacist involvement. Our data suggest a need for continued education to improve patients' understanding of the prevalence of AMR and the risks associated with taking antibiotics when they are not clinically indicated or are inappropriate.
Conclusion

In conclusion, our survey reveals a gap in patients' knowledge of the prevalence of the global threat of antibiotics among patients receiving care from clinics serving low-income or rural communities. We believe that patient education regarding the prevalence of AMR and antibiotic use will bridge this gap and improve antibiotic use. Finally, patients were mostly supportive of pharmacist involvement in antibiotic prescribing, with the few negative comments mostly related to a lack of knowledge and understanding of the beneficial impact of ASPs. Thus, understanding patients' perceived attitudes will facilitate clinicians' patient-centered, infrastructure-supported interventions to improve antibiotic prescribing in the community.

passages.text: JCCG ALL-B12: Evaluation of Intensified Therapies With Vincristine/Dexamethasone Pulses and Asparaginase and Augmented High-Dose Methotrexate for Pediatric B-ALL
PURPOSE
The JCCG ALL-B12 clinical trial aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of unvalidated treatment phases for pediatric ALL and develop a safety-focused treatment framework.
PATIENTS AND METHODS

Patients age 1-19 years with newly diagnosed B-ALL were enrolled in this study. These patients were stratified into standard-risk (SR), intermediate-risk (IR), and high-risk (HR) groups. Randomized comparisons assessed the effectiveness of vincristine (VCR)/dexamethasone pulses in the SR group, evaluated the effects of L-asparaginase (ASP) intensification in the IR group, and compared standard consolidation including block-type treatment with experimental consolidation with high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) intensified with VCR and ASP in the HR group.
RESULTS

Of 1,936 patients enrolled, 1,804 were eligible for the experimental treatment. The overall 5-year event-free survival and overall survival rates were 85.2% (95% CI, 83.5 to 86.8) and 94.3% (95% CI, 93.1 to 95.3), respectively. The cumulative incidence of relapse and postremission nonrelapse mortality was 13.2% (95% CI, 11.6 to 14.8) and 0.6% (95% CI, 0.3 to 1.0), respectively. Random assignment in the SR group showed no significant benefit from pulse therapy. In the IR group, ASP intensification had limited effects. In the HR group, standard block therapy and HD-MTX yielded equivalent outcomes.
CONCLUSION

The ALL-B12 trial achieved favorable outcomes in a nationwide cohort by stratifying treatment on the basis of risk and balancing treatment intensity. This study not only demonstrated that existing standard of care can be further refined but also indicated that improvement in outcomes with intensified chemotherapy has reached a plateau.
INTRODUCTION

Current therapies for ALL can achieve a survival rate of more than 90%. However, considering the long-term outcomes of childhood leukemia, the potential risk of late complications caused by treatment, including anthracyclines, irradiation, and allogeneic transplantation, should be reduced as much as possible without compromising survival probability. Advancements in salvage therapy for relapsed ALL, such as immunotherapy, have shown promising outcomes; however, patients who die of treatment-related complications cannot benefit from the potential efficacy of salvage therapy. Therefore, it is essential to avoid intensive treatments with potential risks of late complications or treatment-related mortality as much as possible.
CONTEXT
Key Objective

To investigate the effectiveness of intensification with vincristine (VCR)/steroid pulses in the standard-risk (SR) group and asparaginase (ASP) in the intermediate-risk (IR) group, and augmented high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) in the high-risk (HR) group for pediatric ALL and develop a safety-focused treatment framework to improve the outcomes of pediatric ALL.
Knowledge Generated

The ALL-B12 treatment regimen achieved excellent survival rates with minimal treatment-related mortality rates. The randomized controlled trial indicated that the improvement in prognosis with intensified treatment was minimal for both the SR and IR groups. Additionally, it was demonstrated that the standard block-type treatment for the HR group could be effectively replaced with augmented HD-MTX.
Relevance (S. Lentzsch)

The ALL-B12 trial suggests avoiding VCR/steroid pulses for SR pediatric ALL patients and refrain from additional ASP for IR patients; for HR patients, HD-MTX can effectively replace conventional block therapy. Future treatment decisions should consider incorporating novel therapies like immunotherapies, given that intensified chemotherapy has reached its effectiveness limits.*
*Relevance section written by JCO Associate Editor Suzanne Lentzsch, MD, PhD.

The treatment outcomes of pediatric ALL have steadily improved over the past few decades. These advancements have been established through the results of numerous clinical trials. The treatment of ALL is complex, and each component of the treatment backbone was confirmed to be clinically significant through previous clinical trials. However, although therapeutic elements such as vincristine (VCR)/steroid pulses in maintenance therapy or block-type chemotherapy as consolidation therapy have been incorporated into standard regimens for ALL, their roles and necessity in contemporary therapy have not been confirmed. Furthermore, in widely used standard treatments, the dosage of asparaginase (ASP) is not consistent, and it is anticipated that dose intensification could improve treatment outcomes. Confirming the significance of each of these treatment elements is necessary for optimizing the current treatment regimens for ALL.

Given this background, we conducted a nationwide clinical trial, the ALL-B12 study, to investigate the effectiveness of unvalidated treatment phases in each risk group of pediatric patients with B-ALL through randomized controlled trials and establish a safety-focused treatment framework for B-ALL.
PATIENTS AND METHODS

Participants were recruited from 144 hospitals and enrolled into the ALL-B12 study between November 2012 and November 2017 (Data Supplement, Table S1, online only). The protocol for this clinical study has been published and is described in detail elsewhere.

This trial was initiated in accordance with the ethical guidelines for medical and health research involving patients. With the enactment and enforcement of the Clinical Trials Act in Japan, this study was reapproved by the certified institutional review board at the National Hospital Organization Review Board for Clinical Trials (Nagoya) in November 2018 and conducted in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Patient Eligibility

Patients age 1-19 years who were newly diagnosed with B-ALL were considered eligible for enrollment in this study. Patients with mature B-ALL, true mixed-lineage leukemia, and BCR::ABL1 positive were excluded. Written informed consent to participate in this study was obtained from the patients or their legal representatives.
Risk Stratification
The patients were stratified on the basis of the National Cancer Institute (NCI) classification, genomic alterations, and treatment response (Data Supplement, Table S2).
Minimal residual disease (MRD) measurements were certified by EuroMRD and conducted in the laboratory in accordance with the EuroMRD guidelines.
Treatment
An overview of the treatment regimen is shown in the Data Supplement (Fig S1 and Tables S2 and S3).

For patients in the standard-risk (SR) group, 30 mg/m2 of daunorubicin:of which four total doses were given in the induction therapy for the intermediate-risk (IR)/high-risk (HR) group:was reduced to two total doses, and the HD-MTX dose was reduced to 2 g/m2 over 24 hours. Early consolidation was intensified using ASP for half (randomly assigned) of patients in the IR group and all of the patients in the HR group. Patients with a CNS3 status were treated as HR patients and administered 18 Gy cranial irradiation; prophylactic cranial irradiation was avoided in all non-CNS3 patients.

Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) during the first remission was restricted to patients with very HR features (Data Supplement, Table S2). PCR-MRD was used to determine the indications for allo-HCT in the HR group.
Random Assignment

A randomized comparison was performed within each risk group. In the SR group, the significance of adding VCR/dexamethasone (DEX) pulses every 4 weeks to the maintenance therapy was assessed. In the IR group, the effect of intensifying the treatment by adding ASP during consolidation was evaluated. In the HR group, the conventional block-type consolidation of three courses was compared with HD-MTX 5 g/m2 over 24 hours intensified with VCR and ASP (HD-MTX/VL).

Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to treatment arms for within-group comparisons. Treating physicians enrolled the patients and were involved in their treatment thereafter. Neither the patients, clinicians, nor those who analyzed the data were blinded to the treatment groups.
Assessment of Toxicity

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Data on adverse events and clinically significant laboratory findings were collected using the NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.0.
Outcomes

The primary outcome measure was 5-year event-free survival (EFS) in each risk group. The events included in the EFS were induction failure after consolidation therapy, relapse, secondary cancer (including myelodysplastic syndromes), and all-cause death. Patients who survived without events were censored at the last observation date.
Sample Size Considerations

In the SR group, the expected treatment outcome in the standard treatment arm was 85%, and VCR/DEX pulse therapy was considered useful if the 5-year EFS rate of the patients who received it was at least 6% higher than that of those who did not. The required number of patients per group (both groups) was calculated as 325 (650) for a detection power of 80%, 372 (744) for 85%, and 435 (870) for 90%, using a two-tailed significance level of 5%. From these considerations, and allowing for a few ineligible patients, we set the required number of patients as 800 in both groups.

Intensive ASP therapy was judged to be useful in the IR group if the 5-year EFS rate of patients who received it was at least 10% higher than that of patients who did not (assumed to be 70%). The required number of patients per group (both groups) for each is calculated as 213 (426) for a detection power of 80%, 244 (488) for 85%, and 285 (570) for 90%, using a two-tailed significance level of 5%. From these considerations, and allowing for a few ineligible patients, we set the required number of patients as 490 for IR groups.

In the HR group, the 5-year EFS rate was assumed to be 60% in both treatment arms. We calculated the required number of patients using a two-tailed significance level of 10%. We found that when the number of patients was 194 and 254, the detection power was 70% and 80%, respectively, with a hazard ratio of 1.6 for one group relative to the other. On the basis of these considerations and allowing for a few ineligible patients, we set the required number of patients in the HR group as a total of 270 for both treatments.
For these estimations, we calculated by the log-rank test, conditional on the enrollment period being 5 years and the follow-up period being 5 years.
Statistical Analysis

The full analysis set (FAS) was defined as the patients eligible for registration, excluding those found to be ineligible after registration, those with duplicate registrations, and those who were misregistered. The per-protocol set (PPS) consisted of patients in the FAS, excluding those who did not start the protocol treatment or those who seriously violated the protocol. The FAS was the main analysis set used for evaluating the effectiveness of the entire treatments. The evaluation of the randomized treatment arms was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with analysis on the basis of the time from random assignment to the occurrence of an event or censoring. We conducted an as-treated analysis because of patients being allocated to different risk groups or receiving treatments other than those initially assigned.

Survival curves were compared using the log-rank test. Cumulative incidence rates were computed using the cumulative incidence function for competing risks. The competing risks were death and cancer for nonrelapse mortality (NRM); death and cancer for cumulative incidence of relapse; and nonrelapse death, relapse without CNS involvement, and cancer for CNS-related relapse.

Interim analyses for early evaluation of effectiveness were planned when approximately two thirds of the patients had been registered. EFS was analyzed using the log-rank test with an O'Brien-Fleming type alpha spending function.
All analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).
RESULTS

A total of 1,936 patients were enrolled in this study. Of them, 132 ineligible patients (those who did not meet the inclusion criteria [n = 126], registration violation [n = 3], or informed consent violation [n = 3]) were excluded (Fig 1). The most common reason for not meeting the eligibility criteria was being BCR::ABL1 positive and/or having the Philadelphia chromosome (n = 96), followed by a diagnosis of other types of leukemia (n = 12) and lymphoma (n = 11). After excluding the ineligible patients, 1,804 patients were included in the FAS. Protocol violation (n = 19), violation of allocations (n = 4), risk group violation (n = 2), and other discontinuation (n = 2) were excluded from the PPS. Of them, 10 patients were treated without following the allocation and three were treated in an incorrect risk group.
CONSORT diagram of the ALL-B12 trial. The most common reason for exclusion was BCR::ABL1 positivity (n = 96). FAS, full analysis set; PPS, per-protocol set.

The clinical characteristics of the patients are summarized in Table 1. Of the 1,804 patients included in the FAS, 1,241 (68.8%) had an NCI-SR status. Most of the patients responded well to the initial treatment, and 1,712 (94.9%) showed good response to steroids; however, 169 patients (9.4%) showed M3 in the bone marrow (BM) on day 15 of the therapy. Considering other results such as genomic alterations and CNS status, 1,107 patients (61.4%) were assigned to the SR group, 459 (25.4%) to the IR group, and 200 (11.1%) to the HR group. Thirty-eight patients (2.1%) were not assigned a risk classification because they experienced events or discontinued the protocol treatment before stratification. Allo-HCT during the first remission was indicated for 30 patients (1.7%). Of them, 23 survived without relapse, two survived after relapse, and five died. Of the five patients who died, three died after relapse and two died due to transplantation-related complications.

The percentage of patients who achieved remission at the end of early consolidation was 98.9%; however, 10 patients (0.6%) died during induction therapy. The cumulative incidence of 5-year NRM among patients who achieved remission was also 0.6% (95% CI, 0.3 to 1.0). Eight complication-related deaths, seven of which were due to infection, occurred during the protocol treatment.

The probabilities of overall 5-year EFS and overall survival (OS) for the entire study cohort were 85.2% (95% CI, 83.5 to 86.8) and 94.3% (95% CI, 93.1 to 95.3), respectively (Figs 2A and 2B). The 5-year EFS for each risk group was as follows: 89.9% for the SR group (95% CI, 87.9 to 91.5), 79.7% for the IR group (95% CI, 75.7 to 83.1), and 75.5% for the HR group (95% CI, 68.9 to 80.9; Fig 2C). The 5-year OS rates for the SR, IR, and HR groups were 97.4% (95% CI, 96.2 to 98.2), 91.3% (95% CI, 88.3 to 93.5), and 87.5% (95% CI, 82.0 to 91.4), respectively (Fig 2D). The EFS of the FAS, PPS, and as-treated populations were similar (Data Supplement, Table S4).

A total of 250 patients relapsed. The cumulative incidence of relapse at 5 years was estimated to be 13.2% (95% CI, 11.6 to 14.8). The distribution of the relapse sites is presented in Table 2, and BM relapse was the most common. The cumulative incidence at 5 years of isolated CNS relapse and any CNS-related relapse was 0.8% (95% CI, 0.5 to 1.3) and 1.9% (95% CI, 1.4 to 2.7), respectively. The CNS status at diagnosis of patients who showed CNS-related relapse was CNS1 (n = 30) or CNS2 (n = 5).

MRD Kinetics and Outcomes

The results of MRD analysis indicated that MRD status and relapse were closely correlated (Figs 2E and 2F). At time point 1 (end of induction), the EFS at 5 years was 90.7% (95% CI, 88.9 to 92.3) in the group with MRD <10-4, 75.8% (95% CI, 66.8 to 82.7) in the group with MRD 10-4 <= and <10-3, and 50.4% (95% CI, 41.5 to 58.6) in the group with MRD >=10-3. At time point 2 (TP2; end of early induction), the EFS at 5 years was 88.7% (95% CI, 86.9 to 90.3) in the group with MRD <10-4, 50.0% (95% CI, 30.6 to 66.6) in the group with MRD 10-4 <= and <10-3, and 31.7% (95% CI, 18.6 to 45.5) in the group with MRD >=10-3. A cutoff of 10-3 was used to indicate a positive MRD in this study, and among the 1,421 patients with evaluable MRD, 44 (3.1%) had an MRD >=10-3 at TP2.
Intensification With VCR/DEX During Maintenance Therapy for the SR Group

We assessed the significance of VCR/DEX pulses in maintenance therapy for patients in the SR group (Data Supplement, Table S5). After an interim analysis conducted in November 2016, the study was continued, and the final analysis was conducted at a significance level of .0500. The post-random assignment 5-year EFS rates for those who received maintenance therapy with VCR/DEX intensification and those who did not were 90.7% (95% CI, 87.8 to 92.9) and 90.1% (95% CI, 87.2 to 92.4), respectively, indicating nearly identical EFS curves (P = .73; Fig 3A). The frequency of serious adverse events after random assignment was also similar between the two treatment arms (Fig 3B; Data Supplement, Table S6). However, two patients who received VCR/DEX pulses experienced grade 3 peripheral neuropathy; none of the patients who did not receive VCR/DEX pulses experienced severe peripheral neuropathy.

Comparisons of the outcomes of treatment with or without VD pulses in the standard-risk group. (A) EFS of patients allocated to the treatment arms, all randomly assigned participants. The standard arm (arm A) is treatment without VD pulses, whereas the experimental arm (arm B) is treatment with VD pulses. (B) Frequency of adverse events in the treatment arms. This figure includes only grade 3 or higher adverse events that occurred at a frequency of >=5% in either group. EFS, event-free survival; VD, vincristine/dexamethasone.
Intensification With ASP in Consolidation Therapy for the IR Group

In the IR group, we attempted to improve prognosis by intensifying the treatment using additional doses of ASP (Data Supplement, Table S7). Three patients (1.4%) who received ASP intensification therapy and nine (4.2%) who did not receive the therapy had a positive MRD status in TP2. After an interim analysis conducted in May 2017, the study was continued, and the final analysis was conducted at a significance level of .0499. The 5-year EFS for patients who received the ASP intensification therapy and those who did not was 82.1% (95% CI, 76.2 to 86.6) and 77.9% (95% CI, 71.7 to 82.9), respectively, failing to reach statistical significance (P = .31; Fig 4A). The adverse events for each treatment arm are presented in the Data Supplement (Table S6). ASP intensification was associated with its related toxicities (Fig 4B). Pancreatitis occurred in 8.5% of the patients who received ASP and in 1.9% of those who did not, amylase elevation was observed in 16.5% of patients who received ASP and in 7.1% of those who did not, and anaphylaxis was observed in 6.1% of patients who received ASP and in 1.9% of those who did not.

Comparison of Block-Type Consolidation and Intensified HD-MTX in the HR Group

In the HR group, we compared conventional consolidation with block-type chemotherapy and experimental consolidation with HD-MTX intensified with VCR/ASP (Data Supplement, Table S8). After an interim analysis conducted in October 2017, the study was continued, and the final analysis was conducted at a significance level of .0989. The survival curves for both treatment arms were almost similar, and the 5-year EFS rate was 75.7% (95% CI, 67.7 to 82.0) for conventional consolidation and 74.2% (95% CI, 66.2 to 80.6) for experimental consolidation (P = .92; Fig 5A). The adverse events that occurred during block therapy or HD-MTX/VL treatment are presented in the Data Supplement (Table S6). Intensified HD-MTX seemed to be safer in terms of incidence of BM suppression and related adverse events (Fig 5B). The frequency of the resulting febrile neutropenia was also higher in the block-type treatment arm (66.7%) than in the intensified HD-MTX treatment arm (15.8%). Moreover, 20.2% of the patients in the block-type arm and only 2.0% in the intensified HD-MTX arm developed mucositis.

DISCUSSION

Our ALL-B12 study achieved excellent survival rates with minimal treatment-related mortality rates. The cumulative mortality rate after remission was 0.6%, which is considerably lower than the 1.4%-2.7% reported in recent major clinical trials.

Several factors contributed to the high OS achieved in this trial. First, as the NCI criteria were used for stratification, a larger proportion of patients were categorized into the SR group (Data Supplement, Table S9). The SR group in this study comprised 62.7% of the entire study cohort, which is higher than the 41.2% reported in the AIEOP-BFM2000 study. Furthermore, reducing the anthracycline dose in the induction therapy and reducing the HD-MTX dose from 5 g/m2 over 24 hours to 2 g/m2 over 24 hours in the SR group ensured that the intensity of the treatment administered was mild. The efficacy of MTX 2 g/m2 over 24 hours in preventing relapse in the non-HR group is consistent with the results of the randomized controlled trial of the ALL-IC-BFM2009 study.

In this study, we eliminated prophylactic CNS irradiation from the regimens without observing an increase in CNS relapse rates. Intensified intrathecal therapy (13, 15, and 20 times for the SR, IR, and HR groups, respectively) may suppress both CNS and BM relapse. These findings suggest that elimination of therapeutic CNS irradiation is worth challenging in the future clinical trials. However, it is also necessary to assess possible late complications of the intensification of intrathecal injections, such as neurocognitive problems.

There were no statistically significant differences in efficacy between the treatment arms in the three risk groups in this study. Even with reduced treatment intensity in the SR group, VCR/steroid pulses did not show a clear effect, as reported in a recent meta-analysis, suggesting that the previous benefits conferred by VCR/steroid pulses in historical trials no longer apply in contemporary trials. The improvement in prognosis because of the intensification of ASP in the IR group did not reach the anticipated difference in effect. Although this intensification of ASP seemed to contribute to improved outcomes to some extent, no clear benefit was observed. This could be due to underpowering caused by the limited sample size. Some clinical trials have demonstrated that ASP intensification is meaningful, suggesting a key role of ASP in the improvement of prognosis. The ASP used in this study was native Escherichia coli ASP. Erwinia ASP and polyethylene glycol-conjugated ASP, which were not approved in Japan at the time this study was conducted (both were approved in 2023), were not included. The use of these alternative agents will further optimize the use of ASP and is expected to improve prognosis. The favorable results in the standard treatment arms were better than expected, which also contributed to the nonsignificant differences between the two treatment arms. We speculate that this was partially due to advances in supportive care and intensified intrathecal injections in both arms. However, the increased ASP-related toxicity observed in the ASP intensification treatment arm suggests that safety will have to be sacrificed to benefit from further intensification of ASP to suppress relapse, which is consistent with the results of other studies. New strategies such as immunotherapy may be required to improve the outcomes of IR patients.

passages.text: The outcomes of conventional consolidation with block-type treatment and experimental consolidation with intensified HD-MTX were almost identical. Block-type treatment, first used for the treatment of relapsed ALL and then introduced for the treatment of HR ALL, seems replaceable with intensified HD-MTX with comparable efficacy and reduced risk of adverse events. From another perspective, if a certain level of treatment intensity is maintained, similar outcomes may be achieved regardless of the treatment approach. This may represent a limitation of chemotherapy; thus, further improvement in treatment, such as the introduction of immunotherapy and/or small-molecule targeted agents, may be beneficial.

In conclusion, administration of experimental treatments to different risk groups of pediatric patients with B-ALL in this multicenter clinical trial achieved excellent outcomes. Strategic adjustment of treatment intensity resulted in high EFS and low NRM rates. VD pulse therapy during maintenance was unnecessary in the SR group. Additional ASP in the IR group did not yield sufficient clinical benefit. For the HR group, conventional block therapy can be effectively substituted with HD-MTX. Our trial demonstrated the potential for further refinement of established standard treatments. Simultaneously, it highlighted the limitations of conventional chemotherapy, suggesting the need for the introduction of immunotherapies and other innovative therapies into current approaches.

passages.text: Research on the timing for subsequent water flooding in Alkali-Surfactant-Polymer flooding in Daqing Oilfield based on automated machine learning

Determining the optimal timing for subsequent water flooding in Alkali-Surfactant-Polymer (ASP) flooding is essential to maximizing both the technical and economic outcomes of oilfield blocks. This study identified eight critical parameters that influence the benefits of ASP flooding and established parameter ranges based on data from completed blocks and actual field measurements. The optimal timing for subsequent water flooding was determined by evaluating cumulative net profit variations throughout the ASP flooding lifecycle. Given the complexity and high-dimensional nature of evaluating multiple parameters across diverse blocks, a machine learning-driven optimization model was developed. This model enhances work efficiency by automating complex analyses. However, predictive uncertainties and limitations remain due to the variability in oilfield development and the potential for unpredictable changes in reservoir conditions, external market factors and so on, which may affect the model's results. The model was applied to six blocks in the Daqing oilfield currently in the chemical flooding phase, where injection schemes, such as extending the polymer slug, were adjusted according to the model's optimized results. These adjustments yielded an increase in cumulative net profit of 224.9 million CNY compared to the original scheme, with a potential total increase of 752.1 million CNY by the end of the flooding process.
Introduction

Alkali-Surfactant-Polymer (ASP) flooding is an effective technique for enhancing oil recovery by combining the benefits of three chemical agents. In this system, polymers increase the viscosity of the injected fluid, which expands the swept volume and improves the displacement efficiency. Surfactants reduce the interfacial tension between oil and water, allowing trapped oil to mobilize more easily. Alkaline agents react with acidic components in the crude oil to form in-situ surfactants, further enhancing the displacement process. Together, these components synergistically contribute to a significant improvement in oil recovery. It has made a tremendous contribution to the oil production of the Daqing Oilfield. The annual oil production of ASP flooding in Daqing Oilfield has exceeded 4 million tons for seven consecutive years, providing strong support for high and stable production of Daqing Oilfield.

According to the laboratory research, reservoir numerical simulation results and oilfield experience, in order to achieve the optimal EOR effect and economic benefits, the development process of ASP flooding in Daqing Oilfield is set as blank water flooding, pre polymer, ASP main, ASP sub, subsequent polymer and subsequent water flooding(hereinafter referred to as SWF). The chemical concentration and slug size are demonstrated and the development effect is predicted in the development program before the block is put into development. However, due to various uncertainties in the development, the actual effect may be different from the prediction in the original scheme. In order to achieve the optimal technical and economic result, the subsequent polymer slug should be appropriately extended to further improve the recovery and expand the economic benefit when the actual development effect of the block is better than the prediction of the original plan. While the development effect is worse than expectation, the injection of chemicals should be stopped prematurely at an appropriate time, and the SWF should be transferred to avoid economic losses. Therefore, it is of vital importance for efficient development of ASP flooding to optimize the optimal time of transferring to SWF.

At present, some studies were done on the timing for SWF in polymer flooding and the oil increment per ton of polymer was used as the objective function for the transfer timing of SWF. When the economic benefits obtained by increasing crude oil per ton of polymer was the same as the polymer price, it was considered that the optimized timing for SWF was reached. However, this index only took the chemical agent cost into account and did not fully take other costs of block development into account, nor did it analyze the impact of input-output ratio and net profit on the opportunity of SWF. What's more, there are no literature reports on the exploration of the optimal opportunity for the transfer to SWF in ASP flooding.

In the ASP flooding blocks already completed in Daqing Oilfield, due to the deterioration of block development effectiveness, there had been precedents of prematurely ceasing chemical injection and transfer to SWF in blocks X12 and N6. Additionally, for blocks where the development effectiveness closely aligns with the predicted schemes, no injection scheme adjustments are implemented; this situation includes blocks such as N5, X6D2, and LBD. In actual development of ASP flooding in Daqing Oilfield, a more common scenario is that, due to the better-than-expected development effectiveness of blocks, the subsequent polymer plug segments are extended to enhance development effectiveness and economic benefits. This situation includes blocks such as B2X, X6D1, and X6D2. In practical field operations, the aforementioned injection scheme adjustments for prematurely transfer to SWF blocks and extending subsequent polymer plug segment blocks both employ a combination of similar block analogies and reservoir engineer experiential decision-making, lacking scientific rigor and quantitative basis. Therefore, there is an urgent need to explore and establish a precise prediction method for transfer to SWF based on actual development conditions, achieving the optimized decision for improving the recovery degree and economic benefits of ASP flooding blocks.

In this paper, by calculating the changes of the total cost and net profit of the ASP flooding blocks in the whole process, the optimal opportunity of SWF in ASP flooding block was established. In addition, a high-precision prediction model for the optimal timing for SWF was established using machine learning technology, which made the work automatic and intelligent, and greatly improved the work efficiency.
Current situation of SWF after ASP flooding in Daqing Oilfield

The basic information of the completed ASP flooding field trials and industrial blocks in Daqing Oilfield was summarized. Blocks with abnormal development processes were excluded. Details of their basic characteristics and the timing for SWF were presented in Table 1.

The results shows that the water cut of the completed blocks were between 91.55% and 98.19% when transferred to SWF.

It can be observed from Fig. 1 that the water cut when transfer to SWF is negatively correlated with EOR per unit chemical agent and reservoir permeability, and positively correlated with the effective thickness of the reservoir. The Pearson coefficients between each parameter in Table 1 and the water cut when transfer to SWF also confirm this observation. Additionally, the absolute value of the Pearson coefficient between the EOR per unit chemical agent dosage and the water cut is as high as 0.905, indicating a very strong linear relationship between the two.

The injection methods, types of chemicals, and other parameters of the injection schemes for all blocks were similar, only slight variations existed in the concentration of chemicals used and the size of the plugs. Consequently, the EOR per unit chemical agent dosage was comparable across all blocks. The variations of water cut and recovery degree curves for ASP flooding blocks with different development effect were depicted in Fig. 2. A more favorable development effect for a block implies a higher increase in recovery rate per unit chemical agent dosage. Under such circumstances, the decline of water cut is more pronounced, the rate of water cut recovery is slower, and the water cut at the end of chemical agent injection is lower. Permeability serves as an indicator of the quality of reservoir rock, higher permeability facilitates easier oil recovery within the reservoir, leading to better development effect. Consequently, higher permeability correlates with a higher increase in EOR per unit chemical agent dosage, resulting in lower water cut when transfer to SWF. A greater effective thickness of a block may imply both a larger reservoir volume and potential oil extraction. The recovery degree represents the ratio of the two. In this regard, its impact on increasing the EOR and water cut when transfer to SWF is relatively minor. However, a large effective thickness of the development strata may be caused by either a thick individual oil layer or a greater number of oil layers within the strata. These scenarios could respectively increase the likelihood of intra-layer and inter-layer heterogeneity, resulting in poorer development effect, reduced EOR, and higher water cut when transfer to SWF.
The research of optimal timing for SWF in ASP flooding
In order to evaluate the optimal timing for SWF in ASP flooding, the evaluation parameters and their selection range were selected first. And then, objective function was established.
The selection of evaluation parameters

The evaluation parameters were mainly divided into two categories. First, five parameters were selected to determine expenditure, which were single well construction cost and depreciation, operating cost, chemical agent expense, management expense and financial expense. The second type was the parameters related to income. Three parameters were selected, namely, EOR value of the scheme, single well controlled reserves and oil price.
(1) Values of parameters affecting expenditure.

At present, when evaluating the total cost of ASP flooding in Daqing Oilfield, the economic parameters mainly taken into consideration are single well construction cost and depreciation, operating cost, chemical agent expense, management expense and financial cost. According to the actual condition of Daqing Oilfield, the values of the above five parameters were set as follows. The comprehensive drilling and construction cost of a single well was 4 million CNY/well, and the period of depreciation was 10 years. The operating cost was 918.74 CNY/ton. As for chemical agent expense, 11508.62 CNY/ton was set for high molecular weight polymer, 6637.93 CNY/ton for petroleum sulfonate surfactant and 2132.22 CNY/ton for sodium carbonate. Ratio of pore volume to reserves was 1.94. The management cost was 378.4 CNY/ton, including 361.41 CNY/ton of general management cost and 17 CNY/ton of safety production cost. The financial cost was 121.1 CNY/ton, including 64.9 CNY/ton of long-term loan interest, 6.0 CNY/ton of working capital loan interest, 34.4 CNY/ton of short-term loan interest and 15.8 CNY/ton of retirement cost financial cost.
(2) Values of parameters affecting income.

In order to characterize the average development level of the ASP flooding blocks in Daqing Oilfield to a greater extent and make the evaluation model more representative, on the basis of referring to the ASP benchmark curves and the development level of the completed ASP flooding blocks, the oil displacement effects of the evaluation models were designed as three levels and the ultimate EOR was 15%, 18%, and 21% respectively. The dynamic changes of the model were shown in Fig. 2.

In addition, under the condition of similar enhanced oil recovery level, the single well controlled reserves have an important influence on the economic performance. At present, the single well controlled reserves of the completed ASP flooding blocks are between 20,000 and 40,000 tons/well. Therefore, the single well controlled reserves of the models were set as 20,000, 25,000, 30,000 and 35,000 tons/well in this study.

Determination of the optimal timing for SWF based on variation in net profit during development process and its sensitivity analysis

Most literature currently considers the cost of chemical agents and oil prices when evaluating the transfer of polymer flooding to SWF. However, the timing of the SWF needs to consider the overall profitability of the block. Therefore, the cumulative net profit was chosen as evaluation indices for the optimized timing of the SWF.

The cumulative net profit of the ASP flooding block is the most direct indicator of block earnings. The cumulative net profit for the entire ASP flooding process was calculated, and the maximum value on the index and water cut curve was identified as the optimized timing for SWF. At this point, the income and expenditure are equal. The net profit at this stage is zero, and the cumulative net profit reaches its maximum. After this point, net profit becomes negative, and losses begin. Therefore, the transfer to SWF must be completed before this point. (Fig. 3)

The findings indicate that when considering cumulative net profit, the optimized timing for transitioning to SWF for a single well with a controlled reserve of 30,000 tons, under varying oil prices, ranges from 91.47 to 97.56% water cut(Table 3). Correlation analysis in Fig. 4 reveals that the factors influencing the optimized timing, in order of decreasing impact, are oil price, single-well controlled reserves, operating costs, single-well drilling and completion costs, chemical agent costs, and pore-to-reserve ratio. Single-well controlled reserves show a positive correlation, while the other factors show negative correlations. The analysis indicates that oil price and single-well controlled reserves are positively correlated with revenue: higher values result in a later stage when net profit reaches zero, permitting a higher water cut at the transition point to SWF. In contrast, operating costs, single-well drilling and completion costs, chemical agent costs, and pore-to-reserve ratio are positively correlated with costs: higher values lead to an earlier stage when net profit reaches zero, requiring a lower water cut at the transition point. The enhanced oil recovery (EOR) index is a comprehensive metric, and differences in water cut patterns do not affect stage net profit. Following this methodology, the optimized timing for transitioning to SWF was determined for 189 scenarios, and the results would be used in the machine learning modeling in the next section.
Optimal timing optimization for SWF in ASP flooding based on automatic machine learning

The aforementioned method determines the optimized timing for transitioning to SWF, but it requires calculating various indicators that affect block development expenditure and revenue throughout the entire ASP flooding process. This process is complex and labor-intensive, potentially delaying the timely adjustment of injection schemes and leading to irreversible economic losses for the flooding block. To address this issue, a high-precision prediction model for the optimized timing of transitioning to SWF was developed using automated machine learning techniques, based on the calculated results of the optimized timing.
Automated machine learning systems

In this study, we utilized the Autosklearn2.0 automated machine learning system, which integrates three key functionalities: meta-learning, Bayesian optimization, and model ensembling. This platform offers substantial advantages in its algorithmic structure (Fig. 5). Meta-learning facilitates knowledge transfer from previous tasks, enabling Autosklearn2.0 to select machine learning framework instances likely to perform well on the target dataset, thereby preheating the Bayesian optimization process and enhancing model optimization efficiency. Bayesian optimization operates by fitting a probabilistic model to capture the relationship between hyperparameter combinations and model performance. It leverages this model to choose optimized hyperparameter settings, computes hyperparameter combinations, updates the model based on the results, and iteratively reduces errors, thereby automating the model optimization process. Model ensembling involves storing multiple high-performing models during the automatic modeling process and constructing an ensemble model. Typically, an ensemble model outperforms individual models, especially when the base models within the ensemble are robust and have uncorrelated errors. Due to these integrated advantages, automated machine learning generally surpasses conventional machine learning algorithms across most datasets. In this study, we employed this automated machine learning framework to conduct a 24-hour run.
Schematic diagram of automatic machine learning process.
Other machine learning modeling

To benchmark the automated machine learning system, this study selected five well-established machine learning algorithms: Random Forest, Bagging, KNN, Adaboost, and LightGBM. The choice of these algorithms as benchmark algorithms is based on their proven performance across diverse datasets and their unique strengths. Random Forest and Bagging are ensemble methods known for reducing variance and providing robust predictions, which is valuable in capturing the nonlinear relationships present in oilfield data. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), as a non-parametric method, was included to evaluate performance on locally weighted observations, which could offer insights into block-specific variability. Adaboost, as an adaptive boosting algorithm, was selected for its ability to improve predictive accuracy by focusing on difficult-to-predict instances. LightGBM, known for its high efficiency and scalability in handling large datasets, was chosen for its suitability in complex reservoir modeling and real-time application demands. Together, these algorithms provide a comprehensive comparison for assessing the effectiveness of the AutoML framework. Limitations of the machine learning model

While the machine learning model used in this study demonstrates high predictive accuracy and practical utility in determining the optimal timing for transitioning to SWF, it has inherent limitations due to its reliance on historical data and the complex, dynamic nature of reservoir conditions.

Firstly, the model's predictions are based on historical data from previously developed blocks, which may not fully capture real-time changes in reservoir conditions. Properties such as permeability, pressure, and fluid composition can evolve over time during prolonged chemical flooding, altering the effectiveness of subsequent water flooding. This can introduce uncertainties, especially when the model is applied to blocks with significantly different or dynamically changing reservoir characteristics.

Secondly, external factors, particularly fluctuations in operational costs, can substantially impact the economic evaluation of SWF timing. Although the model performs well under relatively stable conditions, it is not designed to dynamically adjust to sudden cost changes. For instance, an increase in operational costs may make an earlier transition to SWF more economically viable, while a decrease may extend the favorable period for chemical flooding, potentially deviating from the model's suggested optimal timing.

Lastly, like many predictive models, this machine learning approach may be susceptible to overfitting historical patterns, limiting its adaptability in novel scenarios or with outlier data. Thus, while the model provides robust guidance for SWF timing, continuous monitoring and integration with real-time field data are recommended to make adaptive adjustments as reservoir and operational conditions evolve. Future improvements could include the incorporation of adaptive algorithms or hybrid models that combine machine learning with reservoir simulation techniques, enhancing flexibility and predictive accuracy under changing conditions.
Field application

Using the prediction method based on the full-process techno-economic evaluation indicators proposed in Sect. 2 and the prediction model based on automated machine learning established in Sect. 3, we predicted the water cut timing for SWF in six ASP flooding blocks in Daqing Oilfield that are in the subsequent polymer slug phase. The prediction results for the timing of transferring to SWF using the two optimization methods were similar, further validating the strong predictive performance of the model. Currently, five blocks (X7D1, B2DZ, B2XD, B2DX, N6D) have achieved actual enhanced oil recovery values higher than the predicted values, indicating that their development performance exceeds the original plan. The optimized timing for these blocks for SWF is later than the original predictions, suggesting the need to extend the size of the subsequent polymer slug.

For Block X34D2, located in the distal areas of the Changyuan Oilfield in Daqing, the ASP flooding performance is hindered despite favorable geological parameters such as high permeability. This reduced performance can be attributed to significant horizontal and vertical heterogeneity. Specifically, pronounced horizontal heterogeneity leads to poor connectivity between injection and production wells, diminishing ASP flooding efficiency. Additionally, strong vertical heterogeneity may impede recovery in medium- and low-permeability layers. These factors collectively contribute to the lower development effectiveness observed in this block than anticipated and others, indicating a need to terminate chemical injection earlier and transition to SWF. To enhance oil recovery in highly heterogeneous reservoirs, adaptive injection strategies tailored to specific reservoir characteristics:such as variable injection rates or modified injection patterns:could improve sweep efficiency. Furthermore, advanced hydrophobically associating polymers may increase the effectiveness of ASP flooding in heterogeneous reservoirs, providing improved adaptability to complex geological conditions. It is important to note that for blocks with unique characteristics, particularly those with strong reservoir heterogeneity, the model's predictive accuracy may decrease. Future studies could address this limitation by incorporating additional representative factors related to heterogeneity or by using reservoir simulation methods to supplement machine learning predictions, thereby enhancing decision-making accuracy.

Following the optimal timing predicted by the machine learning model in Table 5, these blocks were transferred to SWF. Due to uncertainties in actual field development, to minimize the impact of any fluctuations in water cut, SWF is initiated only if the water cut exceeds the transition threshold for two consecutive months. If the water cut surpasses the threshold in the first month but then drops below it in the second month, SWF is postponed. Therefore, the actual transition timing may have slight variations compared to the optimal timing predicted. As of January 2024, four blocks should have completed the injection according to the original plan but are currently in the extended polymer slug phase based on the optimization results. Economic benefit calculation

Using the technical and economic evaluation metrics calculation method proposed in Sect. 2, we assessed the economic benefits for the six blocks adjusted according to this study's results. The calculation method involved determining the cumulative net profit for each block under the original plan and the optimized injection plan (Fig. 8). We then calculated the predicted final increase in cumulative net profit by January 2024 and at the end of block development (Table 6). Upon transitioning to SWF, the sudden reduction in chemical costs leads to a significant short-term increase in cumulative net profit. However, extending the polymer slug results in a longer-term increase in crude oil production, leading to more substantial long-term net profit for the extended polymer slug blocks.

After optimizing the plans for the six blocks according to the model, the cumulative net profit increased by 224.9 million CNY compared to the original plan by January 2024. By the projected end of development, the cumulative net profit could increase by up to 752.1 million CNY, assuming stable conditions. These findings suggest that the technology developed in this study has contributed to higher recovery rates and economic benefits in the Daqing Oilfield. However, it should be noted that actual results may vary due to fluctuations in operational costs and other reservoir-specific factors.

Conclusion

(1) The water cut for subsequent water flooding ranged between 91.55% and 97.4% in the completed field test, and between 93.34% and 98.19% in the extended blocks. The water cut during subsequent water flooding was found to be negatively correlated with the enhanced oil recovery per unit of chemical agent and reservoir permeability, while being positively correlated with effective reservoir thickness. The correlation with EOR per unit of chemical agent was the strongest.

(2) By using cumulative net profit as an objective function, the optimal timing for subsequent water flooding was determined for 189 different parameter combinations. The results showed that the optimal timing for subsequent water flooding varied from 91.47 to 97.56% across different schemes. The influencing factors for the optimal timing, in order of impact, were oil price, single-well controlled reserves, operating costs, single-well drilling, chemical and expenses, and porosity-reservoir ratio. Among these, single-well controlled reserves were positively correlated, while the other factors were negatively correlated.

(3) An optimization model for optimal subsequent water flooding was established using automated machine learning techniques for ternary composite flooding and compared with models established using other conventional machine learning algorithms. The results indicated that the automated machine learning model outperformed other conventional machine learning models, providing the highest prediction accuracy.

(4) Using two methods - the entire process indicator changes and the automated machine learning prediction model - the optimal timing for subsequent water flooding was predicted for six blocks in the Daqing Oilfield currently in the follow-up polymer slug phase. The results obtained by both methods were similar, further validating the strong practical prediction capability of the model. Adjusting the injection plan for these blocks based on the optimal timing predicted by the machine learning model resulted in an economic benefit.
